title: What is AOP, how does it work via proxies? Define Aspect/JoinPoint/Pointcut/Advice. How do you create a custom annotation with AOP? What is Filter vs HandlerInterceptor vs OncePerRequestFilter?
shortTitle: AOP — proxies, advice types, custom @LogExecutionTime, Filter vs Interceptor

s1_definition.oneliner: AOP = cross-cutting via proxies. @Around wraps method. Self-invocation bypasses proxy. Filter = servlet level. Interceptor = Spring MVC level.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** AOP separates cross-cutting concerns (logging, timing, security, transactions) from business logic. Spring creates CGLIB proxy subclasses that intercept method calls, run advice (Before/After/Around), and delegate to the real method. `@Around` is the most powerful — controls before, after, and whether the method executes. Self-invocation bypasses the proxy. Filter runs before DispatcherServlet (raw request). HandlerInterceptor runs inside Spring MVC (has handler context). OncePerRequestFilter guarantees single execution even on internal forwards.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A CCTV camera (Aspect) at every teller window (JoinPoint) automatically records start time, end time, and outcome for every transaction — without the teller writing anything. The camera sits between the customer and the teller (proxy), recording transparently.

**One line to remember:** AOP = cross-cutting via proxies. @Around wraps method. Self-invocation bypasses proxy. Filter = servlet level. Interceptor = Spring MVC level.

sections.s2_technical:
Let me explain AOP calmly, the way I would explain it to a junior developer who has never seen an aspect before.

AOP stands for Aspect Oriented Programming, and the whole idea is to pull cross-cutting concerns out of your business code. A cross-cutting concern is something that almost every method needs but that has nothing to do with the actual business logic, like measuring how long a method took, writing an audit entry, or checking security. Without AOP you would copy the same timing code into two hundred methods. With AOP you write that timing logic once, in one place called an aspect, and Spring weaves it into all those methods for you.

The mechanism that makes this possible is the proxy. When Spring sees that a bean needs an aspect applied, it does not hand your code the real object. Instead it wraps the real object inside a proxy object that looks identical from the outside. Every call goes to the proxy first. The proxy runs the aspect logic, then delegates to the real method, then runs any after logic, and returns the result. There are two kinds of proxy. A JDK dynamic proxy is used when your bean implements an interface; Spring creates a runtime class that implements the same interface and forwards calls. A CGLIB proxy is used when your bean has no interface; CGLIB generates a subclass of your class at runtime and overrides the methods to insert the aspect behaviour. Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB for most beans. The single most important consequence to remember is self-invocation. If a method inside your class calls another method of the same class directly using `this`, that call does not go through the proxy, so the aspect does not run. The proxy only intercepts calls that come in from outside the object.

Inside an aspect you choose an advice type, and there are five. `@Before` runs before the method, good for a quick security check. `@After` runs after the method no matter what happens, success or exception, like a finally block, good for cleanup. `@AfterReturning` runs only when the method returned normally, and it can read the returned value. `@AfterThrowing` runs only when the method threw an exception, and it can read the exception. `@Around` is the most powerful of all because it completely surrounds the method. It decides what happens before, decides whether to call the real method at all, can modify the arguments, can modify the return value, and runs code after. For timing you must use `@Around` because you need to record a start time, let the method run, and record an end time, all in the same advice.

Advice methods receive a JoinPoint, which represents the exact point where the advice is running. From the JoinPoint you can read the method signature and the arguments. For `@Around` advice you receive a special subtype called a ProceedingJoinPoint, and the extra power it gives you is one method, `proceed()`. Calling `joinPoint.proceed()` runs the actual underlying business method. If you never call proceed, the real method never executes, which is how `@Around` advice can short-circuit a call. The return value of `proceed()` is whatever the real method returned, and you can inspect it or replace it before returning it to the caller.

A custom annotation makes aspects clean to apply. You define `@LogExecutionTime` as a runtime annotation targeting methods. Then you write a single `@Around` advice whose pointcut matches any method annotated with `@LogExecutionTime`, written as `@Around("@annotation(com.bank.compliance.annotation.LogExecutionTime)")`. Inside the advice you record `long start = System.currentTimeMillis();`, call `Object result = joinPoint.proceed();`, record the end time, compute the duration, log it, and return the result. Now any developer who wants timing on a method simply writes `@LogExecutionTime` above it, and the aspect does the rest. The business method body stays completely clean.

Finally, Filter versus Interceptor, which confuses many people. A servlet Filter lives at the servlet container level, outside Spring MVC entirely. It sees every single request that reaches the web server, including static resources and requests that never touch a controller. It works with the raw HttpServletRequest and HttpServletResponse and has no idea which controller method will eventually handle the request. We extend OncePerRequestFilter to guarantee it runs exactly once even on internal forwards. A HandlerInterceptor, by contrast, lives inside Spring MVC and only runs for requests that go through the DispatcherServlet and map to a handler. Because it runs later in the chain, it knows which handler method was chosen and has access to Spring's context, which makes it the right place to add a correlation identifier or do handler-aware checks. So the rule of thumb is that a Filter is for raw servlet-level work across all requests, and an Interceptor is for Spring MVC-level work tied to actual controller handling.
sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe what was actually happening in the compliance service at National Bank of India before we wrote a single aspect.

Problem 1 — the bank must meet strict service-level agreements, which means every important service method has to be monitored for how long it takes to run, so the operations team can spot a slow compliance check before it breaches the agreed response time. A junior developer started doing this the obvious way: at the top of each method he recorded the start time, at the bottom he recorded the end time and logged the difference. The trouble is there are around two hundred service methods, and now two hundred methods are cluttered with timing plumbing that has nothing to do with the actual compliance logic. Worse, when the team wanted to change the log format, they had to edit two hundred methods. This is exactly the problem AOP solves. We write the timing logic once inside a single `@Around` advice, we create a `@LogExecutionTime` annotation, and we simply place that annotation above any method we want timed. The two hundred methods go back to containing only business logic, and the timing lives in exactly one place.

Problem 2 — the security and support teams wanted a record of every raw HTTP request hitting the service, including requests that get rejected before they ever reach a controller, such as malformed requests or calls to endpoints that do not exist. A controller-level solution cannot see those because they never reach a controller. This is exactly what a servlet Filter is for. The Filter sits at the servlet level and sees every request, so it can log the raw HTTP method and path for absolutely everything that arrives.

Problem 3 — for the requests that do reach real controllers, the team wanted a correlation identifier attached so that related log lines could be tied together, and they wanted it done with knowledge of the Spring handler. This is exactly what a HandlerInterceptor is for. It runs inside Spring MVC only for real handler requests, so it is the natural place to generate and attach a correlation identifier.

In the code below, the LogExecutionTime annotation marks methods for timing. The ExecutionTimeAspect contains one `@Around` advice that starts a timer, calls proceed to run the real method, stops the timer, and logs the duration for any method wearing the annotation. The ComplianceCheckService runs a KYC compliance check for Rajesh's account SAV2001 and is annotated with `@LogExecutionTime`. A request-logging Filter logs the raw HTTP request for every call, and a RequestTimingInterceptor adds a correlation identifier for handler requests. The characters are Rajesh with account SAV2001 and Priya with account CUR3001.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is an HTTP request to run a KYC compliance check on Rajesh's account SAV2001. The request carries a correlation header and a small body naming the account and the check type. Let me trace how the request flows through the layers and how the aspect wraps the real method.

Step 1 — the request first reaches the servlet Filter, before Spring MVC has done anything. The Filter sees the raw HttpServletRequest and logs the raw HTTP line, something like POST on /api/v1/compliance/check. At this stage Spring does not yet know which controller method will handle the request; the Filter only knows the method and path. The Filter logs this for every request, even ones that will later be rejected, and then passes control onward.

Step 2 — control reaches the DispatcherServlet, the heart of Spring MVC. The DispatcherServlet looks at the path, matches it to the ComplianceController handler method, and selects that handler.

Step 3 — before invoking the handler, the DispatcherServlet runs the registered HandlerInterceptor. The RequestTimingInterceptor generates a correlation identifier, attaches it so downstream logging can tie related lines together, and allows the request to proceed. Because the interceptor runs inside Spring MVC, it knows the chosen handler, which a Filter could not.

Step 4 — the controller calls the ComplianceCheckService method that performs the KYC check. But the object the controller holds is not the real service. It is a CGLIB proxy that Spring created because the service has no interface. So the call actually lands on the proxy first.

Step 5 — the proxy sees that the target method carries the `@LogExecutionTime` annotation, so before delegating it hands control to the ExecutionTimeAspect's `@Around` advice. The advice records a start time, for example 1000 milliseconds on the clock, into a local variable. The business data has not changed at all yet; the aspect has only noted the current time.

Step 6 — the advice calls `joinPoint.proceed()`. This is the moment the real KYC compliance logic finally runs. It inspects account SAV2001, performs the checks, and produces a ComplianceResult of PASS. That result becomes the return value of the proceed call and is held in a local variable inside the advice.

Step 7 — now the advice records the end time, for example 1042 milliseconds, subtracts the start time, and computes a duration of 42 milliseconds. It logs a line such as ComplianceCheckService.runCheck executed in 42 ms. Crucially, the compliance method itself contained none of this timing code; the aspect added it from the outside.

Step 8 — the advice returns the untouched ComplianceResult back through the proxy to the controller, which wraps it in a response. As the response travels back out, the interceptor's completion hook may run, and finally the Filter sees the response leave. The caller receives the PASS result together with the correlation identifier.

The final output written by the logging framework looks like this:

```text
14:30:10.001 INFO  RequestLoggingFilter      - HTTP POST /api/v1/compliance/check
14:30:10.002 INFO  RequestTimingInterceptor  - correlationId=corr-77aa assigned to handler ComplianceController.check
14:30:10.044 INFO  ExecutionTimeAspect       - ComplianceCheckService.runCheck executed in 42 ms [correlationId=corr-77aa]
14:30:10.045 INFO  ComplianceController      - KYC check for SAV2001 result=PASS
```

Notice how the Filter line appears first for the raw request, the interceptor line next with the correlation identifier, and the aspect timing line in the middle wrapping the real method, all without the business method knowing any of it was happening.

sections.s6_takeaway:
AOP separates cross-cutting concerns from business logic. Spring creates CGLIB proxy subclasses that intercept method calls, run advice code, and delegate to the real method. The Around advice is the most powerful — it controls before, after, exception handling, and whether the method executes at all. In my compliance service, the performCheck method has three annotations: LogExecutionTime for timing, Auditable for audit logging, and Transactional for database transaction management. The method itself contains only pure business logic. Adding audit logging to a new method requires only one annotation — zero boilerplate.

The critical pitfall is self-invocation: calling a Transactional or Auditable method from within the same class bypasses the proxy because the call goes directly to the real object. The fix is extracting the method to a separate Service bean. Filters run at the Servlet container level before DispatcherServlet for authentication and CORS. HandlerInterceptors run inside Spring MVC after handler matching for timing and audit context. OncePerRequestFilter guarantees single execution even on internal forwards.
